analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan that negotiates lower prescription prices for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2004, placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2003 Medicare drug benefit, private insurers sell drug plans to seniors, and the law bars Medicare itself from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill would have added a Medicare-operated drug plan available nationwide, with the government negotiating prices directly with drug makers and steering patients toward cheaper therapeutic equivalents. It set the starting premium at $35 a month in 2006. The bill never left the Senate calendar.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, who would gain access to at least one drug plan with a uniform national $35 monthly premium and lower prices negotiated by the government, instead of relying solely on private plans that negotiate individually [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans nationally beginning in 2006, alongside the private plans created by the 2003 Medicare drug law [S2][S3].

Directs the Secretary to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce the purchase cost of covered drugs and to encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents, undoing the prohibition on government price negotiation in the 2003 law [S2][S3].

Caps the starting monthly premium for the government plan at $35 in 2006, with later premiums set by the plan's actual per-person cost, and guarantees at least one plan at that premium level [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear lower prices on drugs sold through Medicare, and private drug plan insurers would face a government-run competitor; the administrative cost of the government plan would be built into its premium [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private plan insurers

drawbacks.text: A government plan that negotiates prices and encourages therapeutic equivalents could limit the choice of specific brand-name drugs for patients in that plan, though the bill exempts cases where a prescribing physician finds a substitute medically unnecessary [S3].

If the negotiated prices did not cover the plan's costs, the premium could rise above $35 in later years, since the bill bases future premiums on the plan's actual per-capita cost including administrative expenses [S2][S3].

Critics of a government-run drug plan argue it would compete against private insurers using government scale and could grow into a broader public plan; the bill acknowledges this concern by allowing the Secretary to designate the government plan as the 'fallback' plan in areas lacking private options [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers seniors a concrete, priced option — a $35 national plan with government-negotiated prices — while leaving private plans in place for those who prefer them. The main costs fall on drug makers, whose prices would be negotiated down, and on private insurers facing competition. The main patient-side risk is a somewhat restricted formulary and uncertain premiums after 2006.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2004, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, where it sat with no committee action and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on July 14, 2004, with Senators Dayton and Levin; it was read a first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar [S1][S5][S3].
The next day it was read a second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 639, where bills wait for leadership to schedule floor time [S5][S3].
No further action appears in the record: the bill received no committee markup and no floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and private Medicare drug plan insurers kept the 2003 law's structure intact, with no government negotiating of drug prices and no public competitor. Medicare beneficiaries continued paying prices set through individual private plans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private plan insurers

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sens. Mark Dayton and Carl Levin
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate Republican leadership (108th Congress)
against.role: Senate majority, which controls floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it sat on the calendar with no vote until the Congress ended

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price negotiation for Medicare drugs, which the 2003 Medicare law had prohibited and this bill would have reinstated

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats; the bill received no Republican cosponsors and no floor action in a Senate controlled by Republicans, who had passed the 2003 drug law barring government price negotiation.

industries.note: The bill would have required Medicare to negotiate purchase prices directly with manufacturers and push cheaper therapeutic equivalents, cutting what drug companies earn on Medicare drug sales. Their gain under the status quo is higher prices paid by seniors and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Private Medicare prescription drug plan insurers
industries.note: The bill adds a Medicare-operated plan sold nationally at a uniform premium, giving seniors a public competitor to the private plans created by the 2003 drug law. Insurers keep their role under the bill, but a cheaper government option would draw enrollment away from them.
